theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you start a detail drawing of a steel bracket to carry a 220 V isolator, which information do you need first?
options: The paint colour the client wants for the room
The isolator's size, fixing centres and wall type
The name of the firm that will deliver the steel

Rounded both to the nearest 10 mm
Given the size once, on the clearest view
Left the fitter to measure the part

Each special

options: Tight tolerances make the sheet hard to read
It raises the cost of making it, for no gain
Tight tolerances are not allowed on steel
The fitter will then ignore all the sizes

119 mm to 121 mm

As a square with a cross in it

questions.stem: In CAD, why is a part usually drawn at full size (1:1) and the scale set only when the sheet is laid out for printing?
options: So the file takes up less memory
So sizes measure true at any print scale

So the printer picks the paper size

options: So the drawings never need checking by anyone
So files open only at the office
So all drawings look and work alike

questions.stem: A CAD drawing is sent to a fabricator who uses different software. Which file type is most likely to keep the sheet exactly as drawn for viewing and printing?

questions.stem: Before a detail drawing is issued for making, who should check it?
options: A second competent person

questions.stem: A checker finds that a bracket's plan is wider than its front view, although they should line up. What does this most likely show?
options: The plan was drawn larger on purpose

options: Redo all the drawings yourself
Report the junior to the manager

questions.stem: In the end view of a tapped hole for an M6 screw, how is the thread usually shown?
options: As a thick full circle only
As two thick full circles

questions.stem: An enclosure drawing shows a 20 mm hole for a cable gland. Which details on the drawing should the drafter check against the gland maker's data?
options: The colour of the enclosure

questions.stem: A drawing has no projection symbol, and its plan is drawn above the front view. What is the safest thing to do?
options: Assume first angle, as most drawings are
Make the part from the isometric only

questions.stem: What does an exploded view of a ceiling-mounted light fitting show best?

Each part cut through in section

questions.stem: Why are the original drawing files, with every revision, kept after a job is finished?
options: For spares, changes and records later

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A cut-out for a pilot lamp is marked "22 SQ" on an enclosure door drawing. What does SQ mean?

What do drafters call the pattern of thin parallel lines that marks the material cut through by the section plane?
What is the one-word name for the difference between the largest and the smallest size allowed for a dimension?
What name is given to the thin line with two short dashes between long dashes, used to show a part in another position, such as an enclosure door when open?
In CAD, what is the name for a saved group of lines, such as a standard isolator outline, that can be placed in a drawing many times as one item?
What is the name of the box, usually at the bottom right of the sheet, that holds the drawing title, number, scale and signatures?
A hole on a drawing is marked M8. What kind of thread does the letter M stand for?
A cable ladder bracket 1.2 m long is drawn at a scale of 1:20. How long is it on the drawing, in millimetres?
Which A-size drawing sheet has twice the area of an A4 sheet?
Which two-letter abbreviation on a drawing means "across flats", as used for the size of a hexagon nut?
What do the letters ISO stand for, as in an ISO drawing standard?
A slot is dimensioned 12 ± 0.3 mm. What is the smallest width allowed, in millimetres?
In CAD, what is the name for the sheet set-up where the model is shown at a set scale inside the border and title block, ready to print?

essays.stem: You are asked to prepare a detail drawing of a steel bracket that will hold a 220 V isolator and a meter base on a wall. Describe how you would plan the drawing before you draw any lines.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would collect the facts: the isolator and meter base makers' data with their sizes and fixing centres, the wall type and the fixings to be used, the cable entry positions and any clearance the power company or the specification asks for. I would sketch the bracket by hand and agree the idea with my supervisor. Then I would decide which views are needed, usually a front view, a plan and an end view, and whether a section or an auxiliary view would make any part clearer. I would choose the sheet size and a scale so that all the views fit with room for sizes, notes and the title block. I would choose the datum edges for the dimensions, the general tolerance and the material and finish to state. Last, I would check the firm's drawing standard and template, so the drawing follows the right projection and line types.
markingPoints: Collects makers' data, fixing centres, wall type and clearances
Sketches the idea and agrees it before drawing
Chooses the views needed, including any section or auxiliary view
Chooses sheet size and scale to fit views, sizes and notes
Decides datums, tolerances, material and finish, and uses the firm's standard

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose the views for a detail drawing of a sheet-steel enclosure with knockouts on its top and bottom and a hinged door. Say why each view is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: I would choose as the front view the face that shows most about the enclosure, which is the door with its hinge side and lock. This view gives the height and width and the position of anything mounted on the door. A plan (top view) is needed to show the knockouts on the top, with their sizes and positions from a datum edge, and the depth of the box. Because the bottom also has knockouts that differ from the top, I would add a view from below, or a section, rather than show them with hidden lines that would be hard to read. An end view shows the hinge, the door's swing and the depth again for the back fixing holes. I would only add views that give new information, and I would line them all up so sizes can be projected. The projection symbol goes in the title block.
markingPoints: Front view chosen to show the most (door, height and width)
Plan shows the top knockouts and the depth
Bottom knockouts shown by an extra view or section, not confusing hidden lines
End view shows hinge, swing or back fixings
Only views that add information, lined up, with the projection symbol

essays.stem: Explain when a sectional view is better than hidden lines on a drawing of an electrical part, using a busbar support or a cable gland plate as your example. Describe the drawing rules you would follow.
essays.modelAnswer: Hidden lines are fine for one or two simple inside details, but when a part has several holes, steps or inserts inside it, the dashed lines cross and become hard to read. A busbar support made of insulating material with moulded slots and metal inserts is a good example: a section through the slots shows the shape of each slot, the depth of the inserts and the wall thickness clearly. I would mark the cutting plane on the main view with a thin chain line, thick at the ends, with arrows to show the viewing direction and a letter such as A–A. The section view carries the same label. The cut faces are hatched with thin lines, usually at 45°, and touching parts are hatched in different directions. Bolts, screws and shafts cut along their length are not hatched. Hidden lines are normally left out of the section.
markingPoints: Section is clearer when many inside details would give crossing hidden lines
Uses a suitable electrical example and says what the section shows
Cutting plane line with thick ends, arrows and a letter label matching the view
Hatching rules: thin lines, usually 45°, different directions for touching parts
Standard parts such as bolts and shafts not hatched; hidden lines left out

essays.stem: Compare chain dimensioning with datum (baseline) dimensioning for the row of fixing holes in a DIN-rail mounting plate. Say which you would choose, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: In chain dimensioning each hole is dimensioned from the one before it, in a line. It is quick to draw and easy to read when the gap between holes matters most. But every size has a tolerance, so small errors add up along the chain, and the last hole may end up far from where it should be. In datum dimensioning every hole is dimensioned from one edge or one hole chosen as the datum. Each position then has its own error only, which does not build up, and the fitter can mark out every hole from the same edge. For a DIN-rail plate that must line up with fixing holes in the back of an enclosure, the positions matter more than the gaps, so I would choose datum dimensioning from the edge that will sit against the enclosure's datum. I might use chain sizes only where the spacing of two holes matters on its own.
markingPoints: Describes chain dimensioning: each size from the one before
Explains that tolerances add up along a chain
Describes datum dimensioning: all sizes from one edge or hole
Explains that datum errors do not build up and marking out is easier
Chooses datum for the plate, with a sensible reason

essays.stem: Explain what tolerances are, why they are needed on drawings of electrical enclosures and brackets, and how a drafter decides how tight they should be.
essays.modelAnswer: A tolerance is the amount a size may vary from the size drawn and still be accepted, for example 100 ± 0.5 mm. No part can be made to an exact size, so the drawing must tell the maker how close is close enough. On electrical work, tolerances make sure that holes in a bracket line up with an isolator's fixing holes, that a gland fits its knockout, that a door closes on its seal and that parts made by different people fit together. A drafter decides the tolerance from what the part must do. Sizes that affect fit, such as hole centres, cut-outs for devices and seal faces, get a tighter tolerance. Other sizes, such as the overall length of a simple bracket, can use the general tolerance in the title block. Tighter tolerances cost more to make and check, so they are used only where they are needed, and they must suit the tools the maker has.
markingPoints: Defines tolerance as the allowed variation from the drawn size
No part is exact, so the maker needs limits
Gives electrical examples where fit matters (holes, knockouts, doors, seals)
Tighter tolerances for sizes that affect fit; general tolerance for the rest
Tight tolerances cost more and must suit the maker's tools

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare the flat pattern (development) for a small folded steel cover for a junction box, and say what must be shown on the drawing for the sheet-metal worker.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the finished sizes of the cover: its length, width, the depth of the folded sides and the sheet thickness. I would draw the top face first, then unfold each side outward from it, so the whole cover is drawn flat as one shape. At each fold I would make the bend allowance that the firm or the sheet maker gives for that thickness and bend radius, because metal stretches on the outside of a bend and squeezes on the inside. I would add relief notches at the corners so the sides fold without tearing or overlapping. Fold lines are drawn as thin lines and marked with the direction (up or down) and the angle. The drawing must also show the sheet thickness and material, the overall flat size for cutting, the positions of any holes or knockouts, the inside bend radius, the tolerance and a note to remove sharp edges.
markingPoints: Starts from finished sizes and thickness, unfolds the sides from the top face
Makes a bend allowance at each fold, and says why
Adds corner relief notches
Shows fold lines with direction and angle
States material, thickness, flat size, holes, bend radius, tolerance and deburring

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a detail drawing and an assembly drawing for a pole-mounted meter enclosure, and describe what each one must show.
essays.modelAnswer: A detail drawing shows one part on its own, such as the back plate or the mounting bracket, with every size, tolerance, hole, bend, material and finish needed to make that part. There is usually one detail drawing, or one area of a sheet, for each part that is made. An assembly drawing shows how all the parts go together to make the finished enclosure: the box, door, bracket, back plate, gland plate, fixings and seals. It does not need every size; it shows the overall sizes, the fixing centres to the pole and any sizes needed to put it together. Each part is marked with a number in a circle on a leader line, and a parts list gives each number's name, quantity, material and drawing number or standard size. The assembly drawing may include an exploded view and notes on the order of assembly and the tightening of fixings.
markingPoints: Detail drawing: one part with all sizes, tolerances, material and finish
Assembly drawing: how all parts go together
Assembly shows overall and fixing sizes, not every size
Part numbers in balloons linked to a parts list
May include an exploded view or assembly notes

essays.stem: Explain how a small electrical contracting firm should set up and control its CAD drawings: templates, layers, file names, revisions and printing to scale.
essays.modelAnswer: The firm should have one template with its border, title block, text styles, dimension styles and line types already set, so every drawing starts the same. Layers should be agreed and named, for example outlines, hidden lines, centre lines, dimensions, notes and electrical items, each with its own line type and colour, so parts of the drawing can be shown or hidden and printed with the right line thickness. Files should follow a naming rule that includes the job number, drawing number and revision, and be kept in one shared folder with a backup. Parts are drawn full size, and the scale is set in the print layout. When a drawing changes, the revision letter goes up, the change is written in the revision table, the old version is kept but marked superseded, and the new one is checked before issue. A drawing register records which revision went to whom.
markingPoints: One template with title block, text, dimension and line styles
Agreed, named layers with line types and colours
File naming rule with job, drawing number and revision; shared, backed-up folder
Draw full size and set the scale in the print layout
Revision control: revision table, superseded copies marked, checked, register kept

essays.stem: You are checking a colleague's detail drawing of a cable-tray bracket before it goes to the workshop. Describe the checks you would make before you sign it for issue.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check the title block first: the title, drawing number, revision, scale, projection symbol, material, finish, general tolerance and the drafter's name and date. Then I would check the views: that they follow the projection shown, line up with each other, and use the right line types. I would check that every size needed to make the bracket is there, given once only, from sensible datums, and that the sizes add up to the overall sizes. I would check the hole sizes and positions against the tray maker's data and the fixings to be used, and the tolerances where parts must fit. I would check the notes, such as 'remove sharp edges' and the galvanising or paint. If I find a fault, I mark it up and return it to the drafter; I sign only when it is right. Then it is issued and entered in the drawing register.
markingPoints: Checks the title block: number, revision, scale, projection, material, tolerance
Checks views line up and use correct line types
Checks all sizes present, given once, from datums, adding up
Checks holes and fits against the maker's data and fixings
Marks up faults and returns; signs only when right, then records the issue

essays.stem: A copper busbar 480 mm long, 30 mm wide and 10 mm thick, with five bolt holes, is to be drawn on an A4 sheet in two views with an enlarged detail of one hole. Explain how you would choose the scales and lay out the sheet.
essays.modelAnswer: A4 is 297 mm long. After the border and title block there is about 250 mm of width for the main views, so the 480 mm bar will not fit at full size. At 1:2 the bar is 240 mm long, which fits with a little room for the dimensions at each end, so I would use 1:2 for the main views, a front view and a plan above or below it as the projection requires. The bar is only 10 mm thick, which is 5 mm at 1:2, so the hole details would be too small to read. I would therefore add a detail view of one hole at 2:1, labelled with a letter and its own scale, in the space beside the title block. I would set the views so that the dimensions do not crowd, keep the notes together, and write the main scale in the title block and the detail scale under the detail.
markingPoints: Works out that the bar does not fit full size on A4
Chooses 1:2 (or similar) for the main views, with working
Sees the thin bar and holes need an enlarged detail (such as 2:1)
Labels the detail with a letter and its own scale
Lays out views, dimensions, notes and title block without crowding

practical1.title: Detail and assembly drawings of a wall bracket for an isolator and meter base
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group the makers' data sheets for a 220 V isolator and a meter base, the wall type, and the firm's drawing template. As a drawing office team, plan and produce a set of drawings for a steel wall bracket that carries both items. (1) Together, sketch the bracket and agree its parts: back plate, two support angles, a gland plate and the fixings. (2) Each member produces the detail drawing of one part, in orthographic projection with the projection symbol, correct line types, datum dimensions, tolerances, material, finish and title block. One member produces the assembly drawing with part numbers and a parts list. (3) Each member checks another member's drawing against a checklist, marks up any faults and returns it. (4) Correct the drawings, raise them to revision A and record them in a drawing register. Drawings may be by hand on A3 or A4, or by CAD and printed to scale. Photograph each stage and hand in the full set.
materials: Makers' data sheets for an isolator and a meter base (from the assessor)
A3 and A4 drawing sheets with the firm's border and title block, or a CAD computer and printer
Drawing board, T-square or parallel motion, set squares, compass, scale rule, 2H and HB pencils, eraser
Drawing checklist and drawing register form
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The group's agreed hand sketch of the bracket, with parts named
Each member's detail drawing part way through, showing the views laid out
Each finished detail drawing with sizes, tolerances and title block
The assembly drawing with part numbers and the parts list
A marked-up drawing from the cross-check, in red
The corrected set at revision A and the completed drawing register
checklist: Took part in planning the bracket and used the makers' fixing data
Chose suitable views, sheet size and scale for their part
Used the correct projection, symbol and line types
Dimensioned from datums, once each, with tolerances where parts must fit
Completed the title block: title, number, scale, material, finish, tolerance, name and date
Checked another member's drawing and marked up faults clearly
Corrected their own drawing, raised the revision and entered it in the register
safety: Keep bags, stools and cables clear of walkways in the drawing room
Use craft knives and compass points with care, and keep them capped when not in use
Sit with good posture; at a computer, take short screen breaks
Follow the Centre's classroom and computer rules

practical2.title: Measured drawing of a training enclosure: views, section and flat pattern
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group an empty steel enclosure (a spare that has never been wired or connected) with knockouts, a hinged door and a removable gland plate. As a team: (1) measure the enclosure with a rule, tape and vernier caliper, and record every size on a dimensioned sketch; (2) produce orthographic views of the enclosure at a suitable scale, with the knockouts and fixing holes dimensioned from a datum; (3) draw a section through the gland plate and door seal; (4) draw the flat pattern (development) of the gland plate or a small cover, with fold lines and bend notes; (5) draw an isometric view of the enclosure. Share the tasks so that each member measures part of the enclosure and produces at least one of the drawings, and each member checks one drawing that someone else made. Photograph each stage and hand in the sketch and drawings.
materials: An empty steel enclosure with knockouts, door and gland plate, never connected to any supply
Steel rule, tape measure, vernier caliper and radius gauges
Drawing sheets with title block, drawing instruments, or a CAD computer and printer
Cut-resistant gloves for handling sheet-metal edges
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The enclosure on the bench with the group measuring it, gloves on
The dimensioned hand sketch with all measured sizes
The orthographic views with datum dimensions
The section through the gland plate and door seal
The flat pattern with fold lines and bend notes
The isometric view and the checked set of drawings
checklist: Measured their part of the enclosure accurately and recorded sizes clearly
Chose views and scale so the drawings are clear and fit the sheet
Dimensioned holes and knockouts from a datum, with sensible tolerances
Drew the section with a labelled cutting plane and correct hatching
Drew the flat pattern with bend allowance, relief and fold notes
Checked another member's drawing and recorded the faults found
safety: The enclosure is a spare, never wired: it is not to be connected to any supply
Wear cut-resistant gloves when handling the enclosure and gland plate: sheet-metal edges are sharp
Lift the enclosure with two people if it is heavy, and keep it stable on the bench
Keep the caliper jaws and compass points away from faces and hands
